commentary.seminaVerbi:
David’s elegy treats grief as an ethical art: he refuses to score the dead as villains, and makes public speech a vessel that keeps loyalty intact even when power shifts. That resembles the Iliad’s grief-work around Hector, and the Confucian sense that ritual lament civilizes raw loss into a bond the living can inhabit.

Mark’s scene names the social reflex to pathologize excess vocation: intensity that breaks meals and schedules gets rebranded as madness so the group can restore equilibrium. That echoes Plato’s “divine mania” (speculation), Sufi majnūn as love-sick for the Real, and the Zen trope of “crazy wisdom,” where the community’s diagnosis is less clinical than defensive.
commentary.excursus:
David’s lament is performance with teeth. He is the survivor who needs the dead to stay noble, because their nobility sanctifies his own ascent. So he weeps loudly, tears his clothes, and sings Saul into beauty, polishing the ruined king until he can be mourned without being feared. Grief here is also a political instrument: if Saul is “lovely,” David cannot look like his replacement by ambition; he looks like the faithful son forced into inheritance.

But the lyric cracks at Jonathan. The language slips from public elegy into private hunger. “Above the love of women” is not doctrine; it’s a confession that the only bond he cannot metabolize into strategy is the one that undoes him. Desire makes him honest for a moment, and that honesty is dread: Jonathan’s death is the death of a self David could have been, a life not ruled by throne calculus.

Mark’s scene rhymes in a darker key. When desire gathers a crowd, the body can’t even eat. The family calls it madness because it threatens the household’s control and reputation; they try to seize him like a runaway relative. The “mad” man and the mourning king are mirrors: one is dragged back toward safety, the other drags loss into poetry to make power bearable. Both texts insist that what we most need—love, calling, freedom—looks like disorder to those tasked with keeping us manageable.
commentary.synthesis: Legitimate rule and true mission are marked by restraint toward the fallen and resistance from the familiar. Honor for the dead and misunderstanding by one’s own are not accidents but signatures of God’s order cutting against human claims.

gospel.text: Mark compresses the conflict into a household scene: crowd pressure eliminates ordinary goods, and proximity breeds suspicion rather than insight. The attempt to seize him is an alternative authority claim—kinship asserting control over vocation.

reading.text: The scene is staged after victory over Amalek and before any coronation: David stands in the interregnum, forced to receive Israel’s collapse as news rather than as opportunity. The question-and-answer form makes authority juridical—he interrogates the report that will rearrange the kingdom.
David’s public tearing and fasting formalize lament as political liturgy: the dead king is honored so the living claimant is not a usurper. Grief here protects legitimacy by refusing triumphalism.

The repeated refrain is an audit of power: valor can fall; weapons can perish. Israel’s security is exposed as contingent, and the text refuses to let military excellence substitute for covenant stability.

marginalia.text: Rents and dust: grief performed before grief is proven.
Three blows in one report—people, prince, heir—collapse of an order.
Mountains as witness; the land becomes a memorial stone.
Eagles and lions: royal propaganda recycled into elegy.
Scarlet and gold: the king remembered by his benefits, not his obedience.
Love stated without embarrassment; hierarchy yields to fidelity.
No bread: the mission runs on depletion.
Hands meant to restrain; madness is a domestic verdict.

lines: Now it came to pass, after Saul was dead, that David returned from the slaughter of the Amalecites, and abode two days in Siceleg.
And on the third day, there appeared a man who came out of Saul's camp, with his garments rent, and dust strewed on his head: and when he came to David, he fell upon his face, and adored.
And David said to him: From whence comest thou? And he said to him: I am fled out of the camp of Israel.

And David said unto him: What is the matter that is come to pass? tell me: He said: The people are fled from the battle, and many of the people are fallen and dead: moreover Saul and Jonathan his son are slain.
Then David took hold of his garments and rent them, and likewise all the men that were with him.
And they mourned, and wept, and fasted until evening for Saul, and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the Lord, and for the house of Israel, because they were fallen by the sword.
The illustrious of Israel are slain upon thy mountains: how are the valiant fallen?
Saul and Jonathan, lovely, and comely in their life, even in death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, stronger than lions.
Ye daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you with scarlet in delights, who gave ornaments of gold for your attire.
How are the valiant fallen in battle? Jonathan slain in the high places?
I grieve for thee, my brother Jonathan: exceeding beautiful, and amiable to me above the love of women. As the mother loveth her only son, so did I love thee.
How are the valiant fallen, and the weapons of war perished?

lines: And they come to a house, and the multitude cometh together again, so that they could not so much as eat bread.
And when his friends had heard of it, they went out to lay hold on him. For they said: He is become mad.
